NITROUS OXIDE
Advantages of nitrous oxide (N 2 O) are well established
including the ability to quickly reach its target MAC
value and quick washout. N 2 O does not significantly
interfere with respiratory drive and has no negative
impact on bronchial mucosa or bronchial smooth muscle
activity in healthy individuals. N 2 O enhances catechol-
amine release and does not reduce systemic vascular
resistance or cardiac output, maintaining hemodynamic
stability. Because its MAC value is 104%, N 2 O cannot
be used as a sole anesthetic at 1 atmosphere pressure to
achieve adequate sedation. However, because it is odor-
less, it is often used as an adjuvant at the beginning of
inhalational induction, especially in pediatric patients,
prior to administration of volatile anesthetics. It is also
commonly used for analgesia and sedation for dental
procedures. 276 Its use for labor pain has faded but it is
still used for labor analgesia in some centers. 277
Sedative and Analgesic Effects
Nitrous oxide has both sedative and analgesic effects.
Because MAC is determined as the threshold of an individu-
al’s response to the painful stimulation of skin incision, and
N2O is analgesic, it is difficult to dissect its sedative from anal-
gesic effects. Therefore the sedative potency of N 2O at equal
MAC values is different from other inhalational anesthet-
ics which do not possess analgesic effects. The MAC of N 2O
and other inhalational anesthetics are additive relative to a
subjects’ movement in response to nociceptive stimulation,
but not necessarily when it comes to the level of sedation.
For most volatile anesthetics, MAC awake is approximately
0.3 MAC value. 278 However, the MAC awake of N 2O is 0.61
MAC (63.3%). 278 Even at 50% of N 2O or 0.48 MAC, the
majority of adults may be conscious. Clinicians often use
N2O at the end anesthesia in order to facilitate washout of a
volatile anesthetic. Even though the sum of the MAC values
of the volatile anesthetic and that of N 2O is above the MAC
awake value of the volatile anesthetic alone, this does not
guarantee the unconsciousness of the patient. Awareness
may occur even though it may not be associated with post-
operative recall.279
In humans, the analgesic effect of 66% to 70% of N2O is
equal to that of an intravenous infusion of remifentanil at
0.085 to 0.17 mg/kg/min, or a whole-blood concentration
of 2 ng/mL.280,281 Analgesic potency of N2O can be attenu-
ated by sevoflurane (Fig. 21.22).282 The detailed pathway
of its analgesic action remains to be determined. However,
animals tolerant to N2O are cross-tolerant to morphine,283
and the analgesic effect of N2O can be reversed by nalox-
one.284 This means that at least in part, the analgesic action
of N2O occurs via the mu opioid receptor. Small animals
develop tolerance quickly (6-24 hours) following continu-
ous administration of N 2O.284 Humans can also develop
acute tolerance to N 2O in only 40 minutes. 285 In clinical
practice, N 2O is commonly administered for several hours.
However, it is to be determined whether its sedative and/or
analgesic effects remain during prolonged administration.

concerns related to this gas expansion effect is bowel dil-
atation. 286 However, this observation is based on surgi-
cal procedures lasting 3 hours. The increase in pressure
and volume in a closed space due to accumulation of N 2 O
is dependent of the duration of exposure and pressure

Nausea And Vomiting
Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a common
complication of N 2 O. 287 However, a recent meta-analysis
demonstrated that N 2 O–related PONV is clinically insig-
nificant following a less than 1 hour exposure. 288 The
authors suggested that a minor risk of PONV should not
preclude N 2 O use for a limited time period, such as for
minor or ambulatory surgeries. Even though others ques-
tioned the methodology of the meta-analysis, 289,290 the
trend consistently suggests that the incidence of PONV is
associated primarily with the duration of N 2 O exposure.
Therefore clinicians can take advantage of the beneficial
properties of N 2 O, especially at the end of an anesthetic,
to facilitate the washout of volatile agents and shorten
the time of emergence.
Pulmonary Hypertension
Several studies were conducted to test whether N 2 O
worsens pulmonary hypertension with no consistent
conclusions due to variation of the experimental pro-
tocols. In an earlier study, Konstadt and colleagues
demonstrated no significant changes in PA pressure
and cardiac output in patients with pulmonary hyper-
tension when 70% N 2 O versus 70% nitrogen was used
(Fig. 21.23). 291 The authors concluded that N 2 O does
not have adverse effects on the pulmonary circulation
or right ventricular function, and may be used with
appropriate monitoring in patients with pulmonary
hypertension. This conclusion should be interpreted
with caution in patients with elevated PVR, particularly
in the presence of right ventricular dysfunction and/
or right coronary artery disease. 292 More recently, the
ENIGMA II study, a large randomized clinical trial, dem-
onstrated no difference in the risk of death or cardiovas-
cular complications with N 2 O. 293
Potential Neurotoxicity of Nitrous Oxide
Prolonged use of N 2O can cause nitrous oxide–induced
blockade of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and
can manifest as swelling of neuronal organelles including
mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum,294 presenting
as neurotoxicity 295 with an acute neuropathy postopera-
tively.296 Nitrous oxide also increases plasma homocysteine
levels297 caused by oxidation of methionine synthase.298
As homocysteine can be easily measured in blood, it can be
used as a biomarker of N 2O-induced modulation of methio-
nine synthase activity. After an 8-hour exposure to N2O,
an eight-fold increase in blood homocysteine levels was
detected.299 Increased homocysteine may be prevented by
continuous infusion of vitamin B12, which is an enzyme
cofactor of methionine synthase.300

Speed of Emergence and Postoperative Cognitive
Dysfunction with Xenon
Compared with volatile anesthetics and propofol, anes-
thetic emergence is faster with xenon. It shortens time to
extubation by approximately 4 minutes.304 However, the
shortening of emergence is not associated with the reduc-
tion in length of PACU or hospital stays. There is some
evidence suggesting that, compared with other general
anesthetic agents, xenon is associated with better neurolog-
ical outcomes.305 Therefore it might reduce the occurrence
of postoperative cognitive dysfunction. A recent study did
show that compared with sevoflurane, xenon was associ-
ated with faster emergence and with better early postop-
erative cognitive recovery.306 However, such a benefit did
not extend beyond 2 to 3 days post operation.307 Xenon did
not show benefits in postoperative cognitive dysfunction in
elderly patients compared with desflurane 308 or propofol. 309
Therefore its neuro-protective potential remains debatable
for patients undergoing general anesthesia.!
Intraoperative Hemodynamics and Postoperative
Outcome
Multiple studies have demonstrated that xenon produces
a more stable intraoperative hemodynamic response.
Xenon is a sympathetic stimulant and better maintains
systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial blood pressures and
reduces heart rate. 310 Such a favorable hemodynamic
profile is very unique and beneficial in contrast to most
volatile anesthetics that reduce systemic vascular resis-
tance and perfusion pressure and increase heart rate.
Hofland and colleagues recently demonstrated that com-
pared with total intravenous anesthesia or anesthesia
with sevoflurane, xenon reduces postoperative cardiac
troponin I release and was noninferior to sevoflurane in
low-risk, on-pump coronary artery bypass graft surgery
patients. 311 However, the benefit of xenon as a cellular
protectant observed in vitro 312 has not yet been demon-
strated in human studies.!
Use of Xenon in Critical Care
Sedation in the ICU usually lasts much longer than it does
in anesthesia. Xenon could potentially be an ideal agent for
sedation in the critical care setting, provided that its neu-
roprotective effect demonstrated in preclinical studies will
be confirmed in humans.313 However, there is currently a
lack of clinical trials to determine the outcome of sedation
with xenon compared to conventional sedation regimens
in the ICU. A recent study by Bedi and colleagues 314 dem-
onstrated the safety and feasibility of its use in critical care.
Compared with a conventional propofol sedation regimen,
similar sedation can be achieved at xenon concentrations of
28 ± 9.0% (range 9%-62%).315!
Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
Xenon is a potent antagonist at the 5-HT3 receptor,316 and
could theoretically exert intrinsic antiemetic properties.
However, a previous study demonstrated that xenon causes
an increase in risk of PONV by 72% (34.4% vs. 19.9%)
when compared with volatile and propofol anesthesia.304
In contrast, Schaefer and colleagues recently assessed the
risk of nausea and vomiting among several anesthetic regi-
mens and concluded that xenon causes nausea and vomit-
ing no more frequently than other regimens.317!

Airway Resistance
Xenon has a high density and viscosity. Therefore when
using xenon, airway resistance is greater compared
to other inhalational anesthetics at equivalent MAC
values. The increase in airway resistance with 70%
xenon mixed with 30% O 2 compared to 70% nitrogen
mixed with 30% O 2 was minimal in healthy lungs in a
pig model. However, the airway resistance was further
increased in a bronchoconstriction model of asthma.
Increased airway resistance is an intrinsic property of
xenon and probably not a result of bronchoconstric-
tion. The increase in airway resistance does not nega-
tively affect oxygenation 318 and is not associated with
decreased airway diameter. 319 Similar results were also
reached in a dog model. 320 A human study with 33%
xenon and 67% O 2 showed a significant increase in
airway pressure but no alteration in oxygenation was
reported. 321 !
Apnea
Xenon is the only inhalational anesthetic that causes a
decrease in respiratory rate(Fig. 21.25). 187 There are a few
case reports describing prolonged apnea occurring in spon-
taneously breathing patients, even with subanesthetic con-
centrations of xenon.188
COMPARISON OF NITROUS OXIDE AND XENON
Both N 2 O and xenon are nonvolatile inhaled anesthet-
ics. Their pharmacodynamics are similar, although the
solubility of N 2 O is higher than that of xenon. The site
of action of xenon 322,323 and N 2 O 324,325 are believed to
be the same: the NMDA receptor. However, imaging
studies show that xenon and N 2 O do not work on the
same regions of the brain. 326,327 In addition, their seda-
tive 328 and analgesic 329,330 properties, and their side
effects 331,332 are not the same. Recently, concern has
been raised for air pollution associated with the use of
N 2 O, and whether it should be routinely used in anes-
thesia. Since N 2 O has not been shown to be associated
with an increased rate of wound infections and its cost-
effectiveness is favorable, there is no evidence to support
abandoning N 2 O for routine inhalational anesthetic use.
On the other hand, since the superiority of xenon over
the volatile anesthetics and N 2 O remains to be deter-
mined and its cost is high, routine use of xenon as anes-
thetic is not recommended(Table 21.2). 333-335 !

Summary
Even though the popularity of total intravenous anesthesia
has been growing over the last two decades, inhalational
anesthetics remain the most commonly used agents for
general anesthesia. At least in part, this is due to our cur-
rent thorough understanding of the pharmacology of these
agents and their cost-efficiency. Measurement of the expira-
tory gas concentrations is readily available in any modern
anesthesia machine and therefore the depth of sedation is
much easier to determine and monitor, compared with intra-
venous anesthesia. Thus inhalational anesthesia will remain
in the mainstream of anesthesia practice for the foreseeable
future. Careful selection of a particular agent based on the
mechanism of its action can improve quality of patient care.
Such care will continue to be based on an individual’s needs,
with consideration of the pharmacokinetics and interactions
of these agents with the respiratory system. Further research
into the clinical utility of the inhalational agents is essential
for advancing the goals of precision medicine in anesthesia.
